# Stage 18 finalized

ArcChat Mobile and ArcChat Web are from now on officially defined as:

# **Cloud Continuity + Remote Agent Companion for ArcChat.**

Their core is not to replicate desktop professional software, but to:

```text
See
↓
Understand
↓
Approve
↓
Steer
↓
Continue
↓
Start Work
↓
Receive Results
```

Mobile prefers:

# **Attention / Approval / Remote Control / Result Consumption.**

Web prefers:

# **Cloud Chat / Task / Project / Search / Automation / Continuity.**

True desktop expertise continues in:

```text
ArcNotes
ArcScope
ArcSlate
```

Unified remote calls:

```text
Mobile / Web
      ↓
ArcForges Cloud
      ↓
ArcChat Desktop Hub
      ↓
Professional App Capability
```

And pure Cloud works:

```text
Mobile / Web
      ↓
Cloud Agent
```

Can be done independently while the Desktop is completely offline.

The most critical boundaries finally freeze as:

> **Cloud Sync is independent of Remote Agent.**

> **Local Conversation and Remote Task status are independent.**

> **Device Presence is independent of Device Trust.**

> **Approval is independent of Steering.**

> **Artifact Preview is independent of professional resource Ownership.**

> **Mobile/Web will never automatically upload Local-only professional data just for "remote convenience".**

> **High risk R4 operations still require Desktop Local Confirmation by default.**

In this way, no matter whether ArcChat adds new professional apps, Cloud Agents, stronger Automation, more Artifact types, or more complex remote processes, there is no need to rebuild Mobile/Web into a cumbersome "ArcForges all desktop software web version".

**What Stage 18 has completed here is the complete boundary of the Companion product itself. The next stage, Stage 19, can begin to truly unify the Task, Run, Pause, Resume, Approval, Steering, and Automation that have appeared in these UIs into an Agent Runtime/Task/Automation Model.**

---

# stage19

---

# Stage 19: Unified Agent Execution / Task / Automation Model

This stage is very critical.

Stage 6 has determined that ArcChat is the Agent/Task/Automation center; Stage 17 has made Chat, Agent, Task Center, Project, and Artifact into complete products; Stage 18 has also brought in Remote Task, Approval, Steering, and Cloud/Desktop/Hybrid.

They must now be consolidated into **a single set of execution semantics**.

Otherwise it will be very easy to appear later:

```text
Desktop Agent a set Task
Cloud Agent a set Task
Automation a set Job
ArcSlate Render Another set Job
ArcScope Analysis Another set Task
Mobile Remote Task One more set RemoteTask
```

Finally, Pause, Cancel, Retry, Progress, Approval, Budget, Artifact, and Recovery all behave differently.

This is what Stage 19 must address once and for all.

The original "Future C# Architecture Outline" has laid the foundation: long tasks must return `TaskHandle`; Task Owner is the App or Cloud module that actually performs the work; task status must be persisted; Cancel is a request rather than assuming immediate success; output passes `ResourceRef`; Hub only aggregates task summaries and does not take over execution status.

At the same time, the general outline has determined that cross-App Undo cannot pretend that ACID transactions exist, but should go through Saga / Compensation; write operations continue to follow `CommandId`, `ExpectedRevision`, idempotence, and concurrency checks.

Stage 19 completes the entire operating model on this basis.

---

# 1. Final unified execution chain

From now on, all ArcForges Agent/Automation/Remote/Cloud long-term tasks are unified into:

# **Intent → Task → Run → Plan → Step → Attempt → Capability / Operation → Result / Artifact**

Formal relationship:

```text
Intent
  │
  ▼
Task
  │
  ├── Run 1
  │     │
  │     ├── Plan Revision 1
  │     │      ├── Step A
  │     │      │     ├── Attempt 1
  │     │      │     └── Attempt 2
  │     │      │
  │     │      └── Step B
  │     │
  │     └── Plan Revision 2
  │
  └── Run 2    ← Retry whole task
```

What can happen in specific Steps:

```text
AI Request
Capability Invocation
Child Task
Approval Gate
Wait
Artifact production
```

This model also serves:

```text
Local Agent
Cloud Agent
Remote Desktop Agent
Hybrid Agent
Automation
ArcScope analysis
ArcSlate render
ArcNotes large Agent edit
Cross-App workflows
```

---

# 2. The formal definition of Intent

# **Intent = what the user or system wants to accomplish.**

For example:

```text
“analysis Run 42 and Run 43,
Find the cause of performance degradation,
And in ArcNotes Create report. ”
```

Intent expression:

```text
Goal
Constraints
Requested outcome
Input context
Origin
```

rather than executing the plan.

---

# 3. Intent is not Task

Users can express Intents, but ultimately they do not necessarily need Tasks.

For example, normal Chat:

> "What is Native AOT?"

You can directly:

```text
Conversation Turn
→ AI Response
```

There is absolutely no need to create a Task.

---

# 4. When must it be upgraded to Task?

If any condition is met, a Durable Task should be generated:

```text
May exceed current request lifetime

Requires multiple steps to execute

Has write/external side effects

need Approval

Need to run in the background

need Remote execution

need to wait Device/App/Network

need Automation

Need to be recoverable

need Budget

need to produce long-term Artifact
```

So:

# Agent Mode creates Tasks by default.

Remote Agent:

# Task must be created.

Automation execution:

# Task must be created.

---

# 5. Formal definition of Task

# **Task = a durable, trackable work goal.**

It answers:

> What is this job?

instead of:

> How many times is it currently running?

Task has stability:

```text
Task identity

Intent

Origin

Actor

Workspace / Realm scope

Project

Input context

Execution policy

Agent/Profile snapshot

Budget policy

Permission policy

Runs

Artifacts / outcome
```

---

# 6. Once a Task is created, the TaskId is always stable.

For example:

```text
Task:
Analyze Motor Regression
```

The first run fails:

```text
Run 1
Failed
```

Retry:

```text
Run 2
Running
```

Still:

# Same Task.

---

# 7. Formal definition of Run

# **Run = A complete execution attempt of the Task.**

It answers:

> How was the job performed this time?

---

For example:

```text
Task 42

Run 1
Local model
Failed because ArcScope disconnected

Run 2
Same intent
Completed
```

---

# 8. Why Task and Run must be separated

Otherwise:

```text
Retry
```

Only:

> Change the original Failed status to Running.

So all history was lost.

With Run:

```text
Run 1 Failed
Run 2 Succeeded
```

The entire history is open to interpretation.

---

# 9. The same Task can only have one Active Run at the same time.

Disabled by default:

```text
Run 2 Running
Run 3 Running
```

Execute the same Task at the same time.

Otherwise:

> The agent may repeatedly create documents, repeatedly send requests, and repeatedly call external capabilities.

Users really need to try both options:

# Fork / Clone Task.

Instead of two Runs of the same Task.

---

# 10. Run must Freeze Execution Snapshot when starting

This is the core to prevent configuration drift during long task running.

At least freeze:

```text
Intent version

Agent Profile version

Skill versions

Model / routing policy

Permission policy

Budget

Execution target policy

Workspace / Realm

Relevant input bindings

Automation definition version if applicable
```

---

Therefore:

The user modified it when the Task was running for 30 minutes:

```text
Engineering Agent Profile
```

Does not change the running Run.

Only affects:

# Subsequent new Run/New Task.

---

# 11. The formal definition of Plan

# **Plan = Operational Plan of how the current Run plans to complete the Intent.**

Plan is not:

# Chain-of-Thought.

It should be an execution structure that users can understand.

For example:

```text
1. Read Run 42 and Run 43
2. Compare startup current
3. Identify significant regression
4. Create ArcNotes report
```

---

# 12. Plan can change dynamically

It is impossible for a real agent to know all the steps of all tasks perfectly from the beginning.

So:

```text
Plan Revision 1

↓ new information

Plan Revision 2
```

Totally legal.

---

# 13. Plan Revision must be retained

Cannot:

```text
original plan
↓
direct coverage
↓
Pretending was always the new plan
```

Because user Steering, Tool failure, Capability fallback may change the plan.

---

# 14. Plan change reason categories should be recorded

For example:

```text
User steering

Capability unavailable

New evidence

Retry strategy

Alternative path
```

There is no need to expose hidden reasoning.

---

# 15. The formal definition of Step

# **Step = A logical unit of work in Run with clear goals and dependencies.**

For example:

```text
Read Session 42

Calculate peak current

Create report document

Export PDF
```

---

# 16. Step is not Capability Call

This is very important.

For example:

```text
Step:
Analyze startup regression
```

May be called internally:

```text
ArcScope.GetMeasurements
ArcScope.CompareSessions
AI synthesis
```

Multiple operations.

So:

# Step = Work Unit.

Capability Invocation:

# Actual execution of actions.

---

# 17. Step does not necessarily call Capability

For example:

```text
Wait for approval

Wait for device

Generate final response

Evaluate results
```

These could all be Steps.

---

# 18. Step can form a DAG instead of forcing a linear chain

For example:

```text
        Read Session A
             │
             ├─────────────┐
             ▼             ▼
       Analyze current   Analyze RPM
             │             │
             └──────┬──────┘
                    ▼
              Compare result
```

Therefore:

# Steps can be parallelized.

---

# 19. But the UI does not need to make the DAG into a complex engineering drawing

Normal Task Detail can still be displayed:

```text
Analyzing telemetry
  ✓ Current
  ✓ RPM
  ○ Comparing

Creating report
```

The underlying layer supports DAG.

The user experience is kept simple.

---

# 20. The formal definition of Attempt

# **Attempt = An actual execution attempt of a Step.**

For example:

```text
Step:
Query ArcScope

Attempt 1
Timeout

Attempt 2
Success
```

---

# 21. Retry Step does not generate a new Step

Still:

```text
Step A

Attempt 1
Attempt 2
Attempt 3
```

This way you can know:

> These are the same logical jobs being retried three times.

---

# 22. Attempt must distinguish between Technical Retry and User Retry

For example:

```text
Temporary network timeout
```

The system can automatically reattempt.

And:

```text
Document conflict
```

May require:

# User/Agent re-decision.

Mechanical Retry is not possible.

---

# 23. Capability Invocation formal definition

# **Capability Invocation = A semantic capability invocation of an Arc App/Integration/Tool.**

For example:

```text
ArcScope.CompareSessions

ArcNotes.CreateDocument

ArcSlate.ExportVideo
```

---

# 24. Capability Owner is always the real business authority

ArcChat:

```text
requests
```

ArcNotes:

```text
decides and executes
```

So:

```text
ArcChat Task Step
       ↓
ArcNotes Capability
       ↓
ArcNotes Application / Domain
```

Cannot:

```text
ArcChatChange directlyArcNotes DB
```

---

# 25. Writing Capability Retry must use the same logic Command Identity

This is key to avoiding repeated side effects.

For example:

```text
CreateDocument
```

Network timeout.

ArcChat does not know:

> Whether the document was created successfully or not.

Second call:

Cannot generate a completely new one:

```text
CommandId
```

Then create a second document.

---

Correct semantics:

```text
Logical CommandId
    stable

AttemptId
    changes per attempt
```

Provider:

> Idempotent processing based on CommandId.

This directly inherits the CommandId / Revision model that the general outline has already determined.

---

# 26. AttemptId and CommandId must be separated

```text
CommandId
=
“Create this document”This business action
```

```text
AttemptId
=
How many times is it actually sent?/execute
```

This is something that must not be messed with in the future.

---

# 27. Read Capability Retry is much simpler

For example:

```text
ReadDocument
QuerySignal
```

It's usually safe to try again.

But still consider:

# Revision.

If the objects read before and after have changed:

> The Task should know that the Context has changed.

---

# 28. Input Binding must distinguish between Fixed and Dynamic

For example Task:

> "Analyzing Run 42."

By default it should be bound to:

```text
SessionId 42
Revision X
```

Belongs to:

# Fixed Reference.

---

And Automation:

> "Analyze the latest Session every day."

Then the input should be:

# Dynamic Selector.

For example:

```text
Latest ArcScope Session
matching Project Motor V2
```

---

# 29. Dynamic Input must be parsed at the beginning of each Task Run

Process:

```text
Automation fires
↓
Resolve “latest session”
↓
Run 42 selected
↓
Bind Run 42 / revision
↓
Task begins
```

During execution:

> It will not automatically switch to Run 43 just because it appears.

---

# 30. Event Trigger Input

For example:

```text
ArcScope.AnomalyDetected
```

Trigger Automation.

The event payload:

# Fixed on Trigger Occurrence.

It will not be re-queried later:

> "What's the latest anomaly now?"

Unless the Automation definition itself requires it.

---

# 31. Task input uses Stable References by default.

Cannot put:

```text
CurrentSelection
```

Always save as:

> "What the user currently selects".

When Task is created:

should be parsed into:

```text
specific Resource / Range / Revision
```

Otherwise, the user changes Selection when running in the background:

> The task goal has changed.

---

# 32. The result of Step and Artifact must be separated

A Step can produce:

```text
structured measurement result
temporary data
ResourceRef
```

These are not necessarily Artifacts.

---

# 33. Artifact only represents results that truly have independent value to users.

For example:

```text
ArcNotes Report
Rendered Video
Technical Report
Exported File
Analysis Result intended for reuse
```

And:

```text
temporary token count
intermediate JSON
decoder cache
```

Not an artifact.

---

# 34. Task completion does not require Artifact

For example:

> "Tag ArcNotes Document X."

After completion:

# Task Succeeded.

There is no need to create a fake Artifact.

---

# 35. Task Owner/Authority must be unique

This is one of the most important principles of the entire model.

Each Task only has:

# An Authoritative Owner.

---

For example Local ArcChat Agent Task:

```text
Owner:
ArcChat Desktop
```

Cloud Agent Task:

```text
Owner:
ArcForges Cloud Task module
```

ArcSlate Render Child Task:

```text
Owner:
ArcSlate
```

---

The general outline has been made clear: the Task Owner is the application or cloud module that actually performs the work, the task status is persisted, and the Hub only aggregates summaries.

---

# 36. Task Authority does not allow silent migration

For example:

```text
Local Task
```

Not because the user later opens Mobile:

> Suddenly move the Task authority to the Cloud.

---

If Remote continuation is required:

Can:

```text
Cloud Remote Root Task
        ↓
references / coordinates
Local Child Task
```

Instead of moving the original Owner.

---

# 37. Owner of Remote Task

The Remote Task recommendations of Stage 18 are officially closed as:

```text
Mobile/Web
↓
Cloud Root Task
↓
Desktop Child Execution
```

Therefore:

# Remote Root Task Authority = Cloud.

---

Even though real ArcScope analysis is at:

```text
DEKU Desktop
```

Execute.

---

# 38. Agent Task initiated by Local Desktop

For example:

```text
Desktop ArcChat
↓
Analyze local ArcScope
```

Root Task:

# ArcChat Desktop-owned.

Requires Managed AI:

> Cloud AI can be invoked.

It will not become a Cloud-owned Task.

---

# 39. Cloud-owned Task can own Desktop Child Task

For example:

```text
Cloud Root Task
    │
    ├── Cloud web research
    │
    └── Desktop child task
            ↓
         ArcScope
```

This is Hybrid.

---

# 40. Hybrid is not the third mysterious Runtime

# **Hybrid = Steps/Child Tasks in a Task are distributed in multiple Execution Locations.**

For example:

```text
Cloud
Desktop
Cloud
```

combination.

---

So:

```text
Local
Cloud
Hybrid
```

is:

# Placement / Execution Policy.

Not three sets of Task Engines.

---

# 41. Execution Location formal model

A Step can actually run on:

```text
Current Device

Specific Trusted Device

Cloud

Owning Specialist App on device
```

---

# 42. Task Target Policy

Task creation can be:

```text
Auto

Current Device

Specific Device

Cloud

Hybrid Allowed
```

---

# 43. Auto does not mean you can change places at will

Auto is still affected by:

```text
Data availability

Capability availability

Permission

Cost

Privacy

Workspace policy

User preference
```

restrictions.

---

# 44. Local-only Data must not be automatically uploaded for Auto execution.

For example:

```text
80GB ArcScope capture
```

Only Desktop exists.

Auto:

# Select Desktop.

Not:

> Upload 80GB → Cloud execution.

---

# 45. Fallback Execution Policy must also be explicit

For example:

```text
Preferred:
Cloud

Fallback:
DEKU Desktop
```

User/Profile can be allowed.

---

Cannot:

> If the Cloud fails, it secretly performs external side effects on the Desktop.

---

# 46. Task Status should not be designed as dozens of mutually exclusive Enums

This is where it's easy to rework in the future.

I recommend officially adopting:

# **Lifecycle State + Reason/Facet**

instead of:

```text
WaitingForApp
WaitingForDevice
WaitingForNetwork
WaitingForApproval
WaitingForBudget
...
```

All become independent top-level states.

---

# 47. Task Core Lifecycle State

Unified to:

```text
Queued

Running

Waiting

Paused

Interrupted

Succeeded

PartiallySucceeded

Failed

Canceled
```

---

# 48. Waiting and WaitingReason

For example:

```text
Approval

Device

App

Network

Resource

RateLimit

Budget

Dependency

ChildTask

ScheduleCondition
```

Add this later:

```text
WaitingForGPU
```

No need to change the entire Task State Machine.

---

# 49. Waiting must also know whether to automatically restore

For example:

```text
WaitingForNetwork
AutoResume = true
```

And:

```text
WaitingForApproval
AutoResume = false
```

---

So the UI can:

```text
Waiting for network

Needs your approval
```

Correct distinction.

---

# 50. The difference between Paused and Waiting

# Waiting

is:

> The task wants to continue, but the external conditions are not met.

# Paused

is:

> Explicitly ask the Task not to continue for the time being.

Sources may be:

```text
User

Policy

System operator
```

---

# 51. Interrupted and Paused are completely different

Interrupted:

> Unexpected execution interruption.

For example:

```text
App crash

Machine reboot

Executor lost

Cloud worker terminated
```

---

# 52. Recovery Evaluation is required after Interrupted

Instead of all Interrupted directly:

```text
Recoverable
```

There should be:

```text
Recoverable automatically

Recoverable with user action

Needs reconciliation

Not recoverable
```

The UI can put:

```text
Interrupted + Recoverable
```

Displayed as:

# Recoverable.

This preserves the user semantics of Stage 6 without turning it into another duplicate Lifecycle State.

---

# 53. Needs Attention is not Task State

This is very important.

# **Needs Attention = Projection.**

It can come from:

```text
WaitingForApproval

WaitingForDevice too long

Interrupted Recoverable

Budget approval

Conflict

Partial compensation failure
```

So Home:

# Needs Attention

There is no need to create a fifth set of Task States.

---

# 54. The semantics of Succeeded

Task Succeeded is not:

> The program did not throw Exception.

Instead:

# The Intent's required outcome has been reached.

---

For example:

> "Analyze three Sessions and generate ArcNotes reports."

The analysis is completed but the report is not created:

Cannot:

# Succeeded.

---

# 55. The semantics of PartiallySucceeded

When:

```text
Some valuable results have been achieved
+
Some goals are not completed
+
All cannot or should not be rolled back
```

For example:

```text
ArcScope analysis succeeded
ArcNotes report creation failed
```

Result:

# PartiallySucceeded.

---

# 56. The semantics of Failed

Usually means:

```text
The main goal was not achieved
```

And there is not enough completion to deserve the title Partial Success.

---

# 57. Canceled does not mean "nothing happened"

For example:

```text
Step 1 created document
Step 2 canceled
```

Finally:

# Canceled.

But Task Outcome must show:

```text
Completed effects:
Created Document X
```

Do not let users mistakenly think:

> Cancel = Automatically restore to original state.

---

# 58. Cancel is a request

Continuing with the general principles:

```text
Cancel Requested
↓
Canceling
↓
Canceled
```

Cannot:

```text
Click Cancel
↓
Set the status immediately Canceled
```

The general outline has made it clear that "cancellation is a request, not an assumption of immediate success."

---

# 59. Some steps cannot be canceled immediately

For example:

```text
Finalizing video container

Atomic database commit

External API already accepted request
```

The UI should:

```text
Canceling...
Waiting for safe point
```

---

# 60. Capability must declare Cancellation Semantics

At least:

```text
Cancelable

CancelableAtSafePoint

NotCancelableOnceStarted
```

---

# 61. Pause must also be Cooperative

Process:

```text
Pause Requested
↓
Pausing
↓
Paused
```

---

Not all steps are available:

> Pause between any instructions.

---

# 62. Steps that cannot be paused

Possible:

```text
short atomic operations

some external API

Not pauseable Render phase
```

Task can:

> Enter Paused after the current Step is completed.

---

# 63. The formal definition of Resume

# **Resume = Resume from the current Run's persistent checkpoint.**

Therefore:

```text
Task
Run 1
Paused
↓
Resume
↓
still Run 1
```

---

# 64. The formal definition of Retry

# **Retry Task = Create a new Run.**

For example:

```text
Run 1
Failed

Retry
↓

Run 2
```

---

# 65. Run Again and Retry should also be distinguished

## Retry

Targeted at:

> Same failed/interrupted Task.

Default use:

```text
original Intent
original input bindings
original execution snapshotBasics
```

Run again based on the new available conditions.

---

## Run Again

means:

> Treat this as a new job.

Usually:

# Create new Task.

---

For example:

> "Run yesterday's analysis again, but using the latest session."

This should obviously:

# New Task.

---

# 66. Retry with Current Context must be clear

If the user really wants to:

```text
Retry using latest data
```

This changes the original Input Snapshot.

The product should:

# Clone / New Task.

Do not quietly modify the historical Intent of the original Task.

---

# 67. Difference between Step Retry and Task Retry

```text
Retry Step
→ New Attempt
→ Same Run
```

```text
Retry Task
→ New Run
→ Same Task
```

```text
Run Again
→ New Task
```

This is a very important third-level relationship.

---

# 68. Checkpoint must be divided into two completely different concepts

## Execution Checkpoint

Used for:

# Agent Runtime resumes.

Record:

```text
Completed steps

Pending steps

Relevant execution continuation state

Child Task references
```

---

## Domain Checkpoint

Owned by Professional App.

For example ArcNotes:

```text
Before Agent Rewrite
```

ArcSlate:

```text
Before Agent Timeline Edit
```

This is:

# Professional data recovery point.

---

# 69. ArcChat can never create a universal "system-wide snapshot"

Because:

```text
ArcNotes
ArcScope
ArcSlate
```

Each has its own data authority.

Cross-App Agent can only:

```text
Request checkpoint
↓
Receive CheckpointRef
```

---

# 70. Domain Checkpoint should be created before high-risk batch modifications

For example:

> "Reorganize the entire ArcNotes technical documentation."

Process:

```text
Request ArcNotes checkpoint
↓
CheckpointRef
↓
Apply changes
```

---

# 71. Checkpoint is not equal to Undo

Undo:

> High frequency local edit history.

Checkpoint:

> Clearly define recovery boundaries.

Priority will be given to Agent major modifications:

# Checkpoint.

---

# 72. The formal definition of Compensation

# **Compensation = Perform business-reasonable reverse/remedial actions for completed side effects.**

It is not:

# Database Rollback.

---

# 73. Each Step with side effects should declare Effect Semantics

At least:

```text
Reversible

Compensatable

Irreversible
```

---

# 74. Reversible

For example:

```text
ArcNotes local edit
```

Owner can provide reliable:

# Undo / Restore Checkpoint.

---

# 75. Compensatable

For example:

```text
Created document
```

Can:

```text
Move document to Trash
```

But it is not equal to:

> Never created in history.

---

# 76. Irreversible

For example:

```text
Send email

Publish public content

External payment

Potentially external notification
```

After execution:

# Cannot pretend Undo.

---

# 77. Cross-App Undo Always use Saga / Compensation

Continuing with the general outline:

```text
Step A
✓

Step B
✓

Step C
Failed
```

If the user requests a withdrawal:

```text
Compensate B
↓
Compensate A
```

Each is executed through Owner.

The general outline has been made clear, cross-process operations cannot pretend to be ACID Transactions.

---

# 78. Compensation itself can also be traced and executed.

Cannot:

> Even if it is executed secretly in the background.

Task Trace:

```text
Compensating ArcNotes edit
✓

Removing generated artifact
✓

Unable to retract external email
⚠
```

---

# 79. Compensation can fail

if:

```text
Step A compensation failed
```

Finally:

# Needs Attention / PartiallySucceeded.

No more pretending:

> Rollback is successful.

---

# 80. Failure does not necessarily mean automatic Compensation

Required according to Task Policy:

```text
Keep partial result

Attempt compensation

Ask user
```

---

For example:

> Analysis succeeds but report creation fails.

Usually:

# Keep analysis results

Ratio:

> Delete all results

more reasonable.

# 81. Approval is the execution Gate

Approval should not be interpreted as:

# A chat question.

It is:

# Task execution control object.

---

# 82. Approval must be bound to a specific Action Snapshot

At least logically bound:

```text
Task

Run

Step / Capability

Target resource

Resource revision where relevant

Proposed effect

Risk level

Expiry
```

---

# 83. Approval cannot approve a fuzzy future permission

Error:

```text
Allow ArcChat to change anything
for this task?
```

As much as possible:

```text
Allow ArcChat to replace
12 blocks in Document X,
revision 42?
```

---

# 84. Persistent Permission is not equal to Approval

Persistent permission:

> Policy allows a type of low-risk behavior in advance.

Approval:

> Perform a specific action.

Stage 26 continues with detailed definitions.

# 85. Resource status must still be rechecked after approval

For example:

```text
Approval based on Revision 42
```

Before execution:

```text
Current Revision 49
```

Then:

# Approval no longer valid for that exact effect.

Requires:

```text
Rebase / regenerate preview / reapprove
```

---

# 86. Approval Expiry

Every Approval has an expiration date.

Cannot:

> External actions approved two weeks ago were suddenly implemented today.

---

# 87. Approval Denied does not necessarily mean Failed

Agent can:

```text
choose alternative

skip optional step

ask user
```

Only tasks cannot implement Intents:

Only then finally Failed/Canceled.

# 88. Steering must enter the Runtime Model

Stage 18 has distinguished:

```text
Approval
≠
Steering
```

Now officially frozen:

# **Steering = User's execution direction update for Active Task.**

---

# 89. Steering forms Immutable Steering Event

For example:

```text
16:31 Ryan:
“Stop analyzing the video part, Generate report only. ”
```

Cannot:

> Directly overwrites the original Intent.

---

# 90. Intent always retains the original version

Steering:

# Affects the future execution of the current Run.

It does not rewrite:

```text
Original user request
```

---

# 91. Steering may trigger Plan Revision

Process:

```text
Steering
↓
Plan Revision 3
↓
```

---

# 92. The completed Step will not disappear due to Steering.

Trace still shows:

```text
✓ Analyzed video
```

Even later the user said:

> "No more video."

# 93. Steering application time needs to be clear

Possible:

```text
Applied immediately

Queued until safe point

Cannot apply
```

Cannot pretend to be instant.

# 94. Budget is the first-class capability of Task Runtime

It cannot exist only in Stage 8 Billing.

The Task operation itself must understand:

# **The maximum amount of resources the user is allowed to spend on this task.**

---

# 95. Budget and Entitlement must be separated

## Entitlement

Answer:

> What is the maximum a user is eligible for.

## Budget

Answer:

> How much is allowed for this mission?

For example:

```text
Account balance:
30,000 Credits

Task Budget:
2,000 Credits
```

Task cannot be used because the user has a large balance:

> Automatically spend up to 30,000.

# 96. Budget supports at least several dimensions

### AI Credit Budget

```text
Arc AI Credits
```

---

### Execution Time / Deadline

For example:

```text
Maximum execution duration
```

Future:

```text
paid web/API/tool usage
```

### Operational Limits

For example:

```text
maximum expensive capability calls
```

# 97. The most important first Budget is still AI Credits

Because Stage 8 is already established:

```text
Allowance
Purchased Credits
Reservation
```

So Task starts:

# Reserve.

# 98. Task Credit Reservation

For example:

```text
Budget:
2,000 credits

Reserved:
2,000

Actual:
1,320
```

After completion:

```text
680 released
```

---

# 99. Why is reservation necessary?

Because the user may run at the same time:

```text
Task A
Task B
Task C
```

If you only look at all three:

> The current balance is 3,000.

Each cost 3000:

It ends up being negative.

# 100. Reservation does not mean immediate deduction.

True:

# Actual Usage

Just enter the final Credit Debit.

Unused parts are released.

# 101. Budget is almost exhausted

Task can:

```text
Reduce plan

Use lower-cost model

Complete partial result
```

```text
Needs Approval

+700 credits estimated
```

# 102. Agent cannot increase Budget by itself

Even if the model thinks:

> "Spend another 10,000 credits and the result will be better."

# 103. Auto Model Routing is also affected by Task Budget

For example:

```text
Best model
```

Router should choose:

```text
within policy + budget
```

instead of:

> Spend it first and then explain.

# 104. The actual cost is higher than the estimate and cannot lead to a negative balance

Reach hard limit:

```text
stop at safe boundary

request budget extension
```

Stage 8's "no negative numbers allowed" continues to hold.

# 105. Platform Retry should not let users bear the cost of repeated failures

Continue to Stage 8:

If the same logical AI request is made because of ArcForges/provider infrastructure technical retry:

```text
ProviderAttempt 1 failed
ProviderAttempt 2 succeeded
```

User charges shall follow:

# Useful actual work / configured billing rule.

Valueless repeated retries caused by the platform:

# ArcForges assumed.

---

# 106. Therefore, AI Request must distinguish between Logical Request and Provider Attempt

Concept:

```text
Logical AI Request
│
├── Provider Attempt 1
└── Provider Attempt 2
```

and:

```text
Step Attempt
```

Cannot mix either.

# 107. The formal definition of Automation

# **Automation = Persistent rules for when and with what configuration to create a Task.**

This means:

# Automation does not perform the work itself.

---

# 108. Correct relationship

```text
Automation Definition
       ↓
Trigger Occurrence
       ↓
Create Task
       ↓
Run
       ↓
Steps
```

---

# 109. Do not design an Automation as a Task that runs forever.

Error:

```text
Weekly Report Task
Run 1 = Week 1
Run 2 = Week 2
Run 3 = Week 3
```

Because:

> Run should mean Retry/Execution attempt.

And once a week is actually:

# A new business job.

---

Correct:

```text
Automation: Weekly Report

Week 1
→ Task A
→ Run A1

Week 2
→ Task B
→ Run B1
```

---

# 110. In this way, the semantics of Retry will not be confused.

Week 2 failed:

```text
Task B
Run 1 failed
Run 2 retry
```

Very clear.

# 111. Automation Definition has at least

```text
Name

Enabled

Trigger

Task Template

Project

Agent Profile

Input resolution rules

Execution target

Permission policy

Budget

Concurrency policy

Missed-run policy
```

---

# 112. "Automate this" does not save the entire Task Trace

Stage 17:

```text
Automate this
```

For example save:

```text
Engineering Agent

DEKU Desktop

1,000 credits
```

---

## Fixed Reference

Do this every time:

```text
same one Notebook / Project
```

## Dynamic Selector

For example:

```text
All unresolved findings
```

## Trigger Payload

For example:

```text
ArcScope anomaly event
```

data for this event.

```text
Manual / Run Now

External Integration Event later
```

```text
non-existent local time
```

# 120. Disable Automation only blocks future Triggers

# 121. Delete Automation does not delete historical Tasks

```text
09:00
Desktop offline
```

# 125. Recurring Automation's default security policy

# 127. The true meaning of Replace

```text
caused by
```

```text
Desktop offline
```

# 138. Automation and Permission

# Owner App.

# 144. Agent uses Optimistic Revision as the default concurrency mode.

Continuing with the general outline:

```text
ExpectedRevision
```

# Conflict.

# Stage 19 finalized

From now on, ArcForges no longer exists:

> "Agent Task, Cloud Job, Automation Job, Remote Task, and ArcSlate Render Job each have their own operating model."

The unified model is:

# **Intent → Task → Run → Plan → Step → Attempt → Capability / Operation**

Among them:

### Task

Representative:

# A lasting work.

### Run

Representative:

# A complete execution attempt of this work.

### Step

Representative:

# A logical unit of work.

### Attempt

Representative:

# A specific execution attempt of Step.

### Capability

Representative:

# Semantic call to the real Owner App/Tool.

---

Long tasks pass:

# Child Task / TaskHandle

Combination, rather than occupying the RPC for a long time.

Task has one and only one authoritative Owner; Hub, Mobile, Web, and SignalR can only observe/control it and do not become the second authoritative status source. This principle is completely consistent with the existing TaskHandle design of the original general outline.

Unified execution semantics also formally include:

```text
Pause / Resume
Cancel request
Retry
Run Again
Checkpoint
Compensation
Approval
Steering
Budget
Reservation
Recovery
Progress
Partial Success
Local / Cloud / Hybrid
Child Tasks
Automation Triggers
Missed Runs
Concurrency
Event loop protection
```

The most important long-term principles are:

> **Do not pretend to have ACID Transaction across Apps.**

> **Do not treat Cancel as Undo.**

> **Do not treat Retry as re-executing all side effects.**

> **Do not let Automation become another Job Engine.**

> **Do not allow Cloud, Desktop, and Mobile to each generate another set of Task State.**

> ** Tasks are not allowed to drift quietly due to model, Profile, and Automation configuration changes during operation.**

> **Any side effect must be able to determine whether it has not occurred, has occurred, or cannot be confirmed.**

> **All long-term tasks can be tracked, restored, cost explained, impact explained, and by whom/where executed.**

After achieving this, **Task Center, Remote Task, Approval, Steering, Automations, Cloud/Desktop/Hybrid** that users see in Stage 17/18 already have the same complete set of running semantics.

**Stage 19 At this point, it can be considered that the Execution/Task/Automation product architecture layer is officially closed-loop.**

# stage20

---

# Stage 20: ArcSlate Complete Product Specification & Olive-to-C# Rewrite Plan

There are two real problems to be solved at this stage:

> **First, what kind of complete video editing product is ArcSlate ultimately?**
> **Second, how to remap the product ideas and functions worth retaining in Olive to the frozen C# + Avalonia + Native AOT ArcForges architecture, instead of translating Olive's C++/Qt class structure line by line.**

This is completely consistent with the "ArcForges Full C# Future Architecture Outline": the original ArcVideo has been defined as an independent desktop application, with its own Project, Timeline, Track, Clip, Effect, Marker, media index, Proxy, Render Task, local state, Undo/Recovery, and handles underlying media capabilities through the P/Invoke boundary of the native media library; at the same time, it crosses App Only **semantic capabilities** such as "moving fragments, importing resources, creating tags, and exporting" are provided, and bare GPU handles and internal mutable objects cannot be exposed.

Stage 20 will officially upgrade this skeleton to **ArcSlate**.

---

# 1. First freeze Olive's real role in ArcSlate

The current Olive repository still describes itself as an open-source NLE for Windows/macOS/Linux and explicitly marks the existing 0.1/0.2 builds as alpha/unstable; its website still shows "Olive will return". Olive is therefore valuable, but **cannot serve as the authoritative source for ArcSlate's long-term product specification or runtime architecture**. ([GitHub][1])

So it's officially frozen:

# **Olive = Product & Behavior Reference**

instead of:

# **ArcSlate Runtime Architecture**

ArcSlate was rewritten while studying Olive's:

```text
Workflow
Timeline Operation
project organization
Viewer
Effect / Compositing thoughts
Node-based processing thoughts
Caching
Color workflow
Keyboard workflow
Professional NLE User experience
```

But re-create:

```text
ArcSlate Domain

ArcSlate Application

ArcSlate Avalonia UI

ArcSlate Media Runtime

ArcSlate Project Format

ArcSlate Undo / Recovery

ArcSlate Task

ArcSlate Capability
```

---

# 2. Absolutely no "class-to-class translation"

Wrong Rewrite:

```text
Olive::Project
→ ArcSlateProject.cs

Olive::TimelineWidget
→ TimelineControl.cs

Olive::Node
→ Node.cs
```

Then move the Qt signal/slot, OpenGL object relationship, and C++ ownership as they are.

The correct one is:

```text
Olive behavior / use case
        ↓
Extract product semantics
        ↓
ArcSlate Domain model
        ↓
ArcForges architecture
        ↓
C# implementation
```

So what we inherit is:

# **Product Intent, not Implementation Shape.**

The Olive official repository still clearly reflects the original technical background of C++, Qt, OpenGL, etc.; these are the implementation backgrounds that need to be understood when studying the source code, not the structure that ArcSlate must continue to maintain. ([GitHub][1])

---

# 3. ArcSlate final product definition

Officially frozen:

# **ArcSlate = Local-first Professional Non-linear Video Editing Workspace**

It is a:

> **A local-first video editor with traditional Track-based NLE as the core, supporting professional Timeline editing, media management, audio and video processing, Effect/Compositing, Keyframe, Color, Proxy, Render/Export, and native support for ArcChat Agent semantic editing.**

Core workflow:

```text
Import / Link Media
        ↓
Organize
        ↓
Create Sequence
        ↓
Edit Timeline
        ↓
Effects / Animation / Audio / Color
        ↓
Review
        ↓
Render / Export
```

AI/Agent is:

# Enhance editing capabilities.

Not:

# Replaces Timeline Editor.

---

ArcSlate should not initially attempt to copy:

```text
Premiere

```

Full functionality.

Correct positioning:

# **Focused Professional NLE**

Prioritize:

```text

stable Playback
high quality Export

Professional Effect
Color Basics
Audio Basics
ArcChat Agent
```

Do it well.

Advanced:

```text
complete Motion Graphics

complete 3D compositor

Professional collaborative film review platform
```

Not early core.

# 5. ArcSlate's most important product principles

## Principle 1: Non-destructive Editing

All normal edits:

```text
Trim
Split
Move
Speed
Effect
Color
Audio
```

Neither modify the original media.

---

## Principle 2: Source Media ≠ Timeline Clip

a:

```text
video.mp4
```

is:

# Media Asset.

Appears 20 times on Timeline:

is:

# 20 Clip Instances.

---

## Principle 3: Project ≠ Media Folder

Project management:

```text
Sequences
Media references
Editing state
Effects
Markers
Render settings
```

But:

> There is no requirement that all original media be physically moved into the Project folder.

---

## Principle 4: Playback ≠ Final Render

Playback:

# Real-time priority.

Render:

# Correctness and quality take precedence.

Not for smooth Preview:

> Permanently reduces final export quality.

---

## Principle 5: Proxy ≠ Original

Proxy is just:

# Derived Representation.

One can never sneak into being the ultimate original media authority.

---

## Principle 6: Timeline State Owned by ArcSlate

ArcChat can only:

```text
query
request edit
start render
```

Cannot hold a second writable Timeline.

# **Project = ArcSlate's long-term editing work container.**

It has:

```text
Project-level metadata
```

```text
a certain one video file
```

# Timeline.

# 11. Sequence can be used as the Source of another Sequence

This is recommended to be supported directly from the Domain layer.

That is:

# Nested Sequence.

For example:

```text
Sequence:
Intro
```

Put as Clip:

```text
Sequence:
Main Video
```

This naturally supports future:

```text
Compound Clips
Nested edits
Reusable segments
```

No need to invent another media type.

---

# 12. The formal role of Media Library

Media Library management:

```text
Video
Audio
Image
Sequence
Generated Media
Subtitle assets
```

User passes:

```text
Bins
Folders / Collections
Search
Tags
Metadata
```

organization.

---

# 13. Bin is a logical organization, not a file system Folder

For example:

```text
Project
└── Interviews
```

Just:

# ArcSlate Project Organization.

Move the Media Asset to another Bin:

> Video files on the hard drive are not moved.

---

# 14. Formal definition of Media Asset

# **MediaAsset = ArcSlate A stable logical identity for a usable media source.**

It can at least mean:

```text
Video

Audio

Image

Sequence

Generated Media
```

---

It has:

```text
AssetId

Source reference

Media metadata

Streams

Duration

Availability

Proxy state

Color metadata

Import origin
```

Domain design follows specific fields.

---

# 15. MediaAsset ≠ File

This is an important inequality.

Because a media file:

```text
camera001.mov
```

May have both:

```text
1 video stream
8 audio streams
metadata
timecode
```

And Sequence:

> Not an external File at all.

So ArcSlate cannot model the Domain core as:

```text
FilePath
```

---

# 16. The original media uses External Reference by default.

This is completely consistent with Stage 9's design for large media.

For the video editor, the user imports:

```text
200 GB footage
```

The default should be:

# Link / Reference Original.

instead of:

> Copy another 200GB to the ArcSlate data directory.

---

# 17. But Managed Media must be provided

Users can choose:

```text
Copy into Project Media
```

At this time ArcSlate really has:

# Managed Asset.

---

Therefore always distinguish:

```text
External Original

Managed Original
```

---

# 18. Collect/Consolidate Project

Must become a long-term formal capability.

After users complete the Project, they can:

# Collect Project Media.

What will be used:

```text
External assets
```

Copied to a complete removable collection.

This is useful for:

```text
Backup
Archive
Move computer
Delivery
```

Very important.

---

# 19. AssetId is never equal to File Path

User:

```text
D:\Footage\A.mov
```

Move to:

```text
E:\Archive\A.mov
```

After relinking:

# The same MediaAsset.

Timeline Clips cannot be completely recreated.

---

# 20. Offline Media is in normal product status

If External Media is not found:

```text
Media Offline
```

Project:

# Still open.

Timeline:

# Maintain structure.

Clip:

# Reserved.

---

Cannot:

> If the video cannot be found, the entire Project cannot be opened.

---

# 21. Relink is a first-level ability

Support:

```text
Locate file

Relink one

Relink folder

Find automatically

Relink by media identity
```

---

Matching should not rely solely on:

# File name.

Should be able to take advantage of:

```text
size
duration
metadata
content fingerprint/hash when available
```

Specific Stage 22 design.

---

# 22. Time Model must be frozen now

This is one of the worst things about video editing software that you cannot rework later.

# **Any Timeline core time cannot use `double seconds` as the authoritative time.**

---

Must use:

# Integer/Rational Time Model.

Logically:

```text
TimeValue + TimeBase
```

Or an equivalent exact model.

---

# 23. Why cannot we use floating point seconds?

Because it must be handled correctly:

```text
23.976

29.97

59.94

audio samples

source timebases

long timelines
```

Floating point cumulative errors will later result in:

```text
frame drift
A/V sync
trim boundary error
```

---

# 24. Video and Audio time precision must coexist

Video editing:

# Frame precision.

Audio:

# Sample precision.

Therefore, the Timeline overall time system cannot:

> Can only represent Frame Number.

Otherwise, the detailed Audio Edit will have to be reworked later.

---

# 25. Sequence Frame Rate uses Rational

For example logic:

```text
24000 / 1001

30000 / 1001
```

instead of:

```text
23.976
29.97
```

as authoritative data.

---

# 26. Separation of Source Time and Timeline Time

A Clip at least logically exists:

```text
Timeline Start

Timeline Duration

Source In

Source Out
```

---

For example:

```text
Source:
10:00 – 20:00

Timeline:
01:30 – 01:40
```

Completely independent.

---

# 27. Formal definition of Clip

# **Clip = A non-destructive instantiation of a Source/Asset on the Sequence Timeline.**

It is not the media itself.

---

The core semantics possessed by Clip include:

```text
Source reference

Timeline placement

Source range

Time mapping / speed

Effects

Opacity / gain where applicable

Link group

State
```

---

# 28. The same Asset can have unlimited Clips

This is the basis of NLE.

For example:

```text
Asset A
├── Clip A1
├── Clip A2
├── Clip A3
└── Clip A4
```

Each:

```text
different In/Out
different Effect
different Speed
```

---

# 29. ClipId must be stable

Normal Trim:

> Clips should not be deleted and new ones created.

Otherwise:

```text
Agent reference
Marker relation
Undo
Effect
Selection
```

will become unstable.

---

# 30. Formal model of Track

It is recommended to have at least three main Track Roles:

```text
Video Track

Audio Track

Subtitle / Caption Track
```

---

Special Tracks can be expanded in the future.

But do not hardcode all Tracks into:

```text
VideoTrack1
VideoTrack2
AudioTrack1
```

Different C# classes proliferate everywhere.

---

# 31. Traditional Track-based Timeline officially frozen

ArcSlate maintains:

# Familiar Professional Track-based NLE.

The basic Timeline is not turned into a completely different Magnetic Timeline Paradigm like Final Cut.

---

Can provide:

```text
Ripple editing
Snapping
Linked selection
```

Improve efficiency.

But the basic spatial model is still:

```text
Tracks
+
Timeline positions
```

---

# 32. Basic Timeline operations must be complete

Long-term official support:

```text
Insert

Overwrite

Move

Split

Delete

Ripple Delete

Lift

Extract

Trim

Ripple Trim

Roll

Slip

Slide
```

This set belongs to the NLE core.

# 33. These must be semantic commands

For example:

```text
RippleTrimClip
```

instead of:

This way:

```text
UI
Keyboard

Undo
```

This is exactly the application where the ArcForges general outline requires that "local UI and remote semantic calls ultimately follow the same application service path."

# 34. Snap is a Timeline Service, not a mouse Hack

```text
Other clip edges
```

Snap:

```text
+
```

should become a formal concept.

association.

by:

# 51. Effect Stack does not create a second set of Effect Model

```text
↓
Color
↓
Transform
```

```text
linear graph
```

```text
Stack Effect Engine

and
```

# 52. This is also Olive's product idea worthy of reference.

Olive's official repository and project history have always focused on media processing capabilities such as NLE, OpenGL/GLSL, and effects; the project community also continues to discuss workflows such as Node Editor and Effect. We retain the idea that node-based processing deserves a high-level capability, but re-establish the ArcSlate model as typed, versioned, AOT-compatible. ([GitHub][1])

# 193. Olive-to-ArcSlate Migration Matrix

The final recommendations are as follows:

| Olive direction/thoughts                          | ArcSlateDecision                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Cross-platform NLE                  | **RESERVED**                       |
| Project / Sequence / Timeline       | **Keep and remodel**                  |
| Track-based editing                 | **RESERVED**                       |
| Node-based processing               | **Reserved for Advanced Processing Graph**   |
| Effect editing                      | **Keep and provide simplified Inspector**        |
| Keyframe animation                  | **Keep/Perfect**                    |
| Caching                             | **Keep and split into explicit Derived Cache types** |
| Color management                    | **Retain and upgrade to first-class project ability**             |
| Audio editing                       | **Retain and improve basic professional abilities**              |
| Qt UI architecture                  | **Discard**                       |
| C++ Domain ownership                | **Discard**                       |
| OpenGL-specific product assumptions | **Not inherited as product Domain**            |
| Olive project format as long-term authority          | **Discard**                       |
| Olive project import                | **Planning compatible import**                   |
| Original implementation object life cycle                           | **Not inherited**                      |
| UI events are business operations                           | **Changed to Semantic Command**      |
| Original plug-in/dynamic implementation                          | **Redesigned as Stage 24/AOT**     |

Regarding the current project status of Olive, the official repository still calls it alpha/unstable, so the so-called "retention" here refers to retaining its NLE product concept worth learning, rather than treating a certain current Olive 0.2 behavior as a compatible specification that ArcSlate can never change. ([GitHub][1])

61. Project recovery.
62. Timeline structure is correct.
63. Agent editor generates Checkpoint.
64. Restore.

## Render

65. Start Render Revision 42.
66. The user continues editing to Revision 46.
67. Render still uses 42.
68. Next time Render uses 46.
69. Cancel.
70. Partial batch failure.
71. Artifact is correct.

## Cloud

72. Project sync.
73. External originals are not uploaded.
74. Open metadata on another device.
75. Media Offline.
76. Cloud Proxy is available.
77. Rough edit.
78. Relink local Original.

## ArcChat

79. Ask ArcChat Current Selection.
80. Query Timeline.
81. Add markers.
82. Trim Clip.
83. Checkpoint/Preview first for large batch Ripple edits.
84. Render Task.
85. Mobile to view Render progress.
86. ArcChat does not obtain the GPU/frame object directly.

## Olive Migration

87. Import supported Olive project.
88. Clips are mapped correctly.
89. Unsupported effect generates reports.
90. Project can still be opened.
91. After conversion, save it as ArcSlate Native Project.
92. The follow-up does not rely on the Olive format at all.

---

# Stage 20 finalized

ArcSlate is from now on officially defined as:

# **A Local-first Professional NLE completely rebuilt in C# + Avalonia.**

Olive is:

# **A great reference source for product ideas, features, and workflows.**

But ArcSlate's authoritative model is re-established as:

```text
Project
  ↓
Media Library
  ↓
Media Asset
  ↓
Sequence
  ↓
Track
  ↓
Clip / Transition / Title / Subtitle
  ↓
Processing Graph / Effects / Keyframes
  ↓
Playback
  ↓
Render
```

Among the most critical long-term decisions are:

### Timeline

Adopt:

# **Traditional Track-based, Non-destructive NLE.**

### Time

Adopt:

# **Exact Integer/Rational Time Model, not floating point seconds.**

### Media

Adopt:

# **Stable Asset Identity + External/Managed Media separation.**

### Effects

Adopt:

# **A Typed Processing Graph.**

Ordinary users operate through Effect Stack/Inspector, and advanced users operate through Node Graph, **not two sets of Effect Engine**.

### Performance

Clear separation:

```text
Original
Proxy
Render Cache
Thumbnail/Waveform Cache
```

All Cache is Derived only.

### Playback / Export

:

# Preview emphasizes real-time, and Final Render emphasizes correctness;

Both share the same Processing Semantics.

### Reliability

:

# Autosave + Undo + Revision + Checkpoint + Crash Recovery

Start with the core, not finish last.

### Agent

ArcChat can only pass:

# Semantic Timeline Capabilities

Operation:

```text
ImportMedia
MoveClip
TrimClip
SplitClip
CreateMarker
ApplyEffect
StartRender
```

Never click remotely on the ArcSlate UI.

### Cloud

:

# Project Sync ≠ Original Media Upload.

External Originals stay on the user's local machine by default; whether Proxy and Original enter the Cloud is explicitly chosen by the user.

---

The rewriting principle of **Olive → ArcSlate** is ultimately:

# **Preserve the editing ideas. Rebuild the product model.**

Not:

# **Translate the C++ application into C#.**

The current Olive official repository itself is still clearly in the alpha/unstable state, so this approach is more reasonable than freezing the current Olive implementation details into the ArcSlate permanent compatibility specification. ([GitHub][1])

This way no matter how ArcSlate continues to grow in the future:

```text
Multicam
Compound Editing
Advanced Color
Advanced Audio
Motion Graphics
Tracking
More Effects
Third-party Nodes
Cloud collaboration
AI rough-cut
AI subtitle
Scene analysis
```

All of them can be built on the now-frozen **Project / Asset / Sequence / Track / Clip / Processing Graph / Task / Resource** model, without having to overturn the underlying video editing domain.

**Stage 20 At this point, ArcSlate's product definition and Olive → full C# rewriting direction can be considered officially closed.**

[1]: https://github.com/olive-editor/olive?utm_source=chatgpt.com "GitHub - olive-editor/olive: Free open-source non-linear video editor · GitHub"
[2]: https://github.com/orgs/olive-editor/repositories?utm_source=chatgpt.com "olive-editor repositories · GitHub"

# stage21

---

# Stage 21: Cross-App Semantic Capability & Resource Model

This stage is very important, because the four products, ArcChat Agent, Task/Automation, Mobile/Web, and ArcSlate, have been fully defined in the previous Stages 13 to 20.

Now the **common business language** between these products must be frozen all at once.

No more answers at this stage:

> StreamJsonRpc uses Named Pipe or UDS?

Nor will it be re-discussed:

> How to configure Refit / SignalR / MessagePack / AOT?

The "Full C# General Outline" has laid out the technical foundations such as Transport, discovery, instance registration, strongly typed RPC, Revision, CommandId, TaskHandle, error model, etc., and clearly stipulates that cross-application calls must be **semantic capabilities rather than UI operations**, and large resources can only cross boundaries through references such as `ResourceRef`.

What Stage 21 really solves is:

# **What common concepts do ArcChat, ArcNotes, ArcScope, and ArcSlate use to understand each other?**

Final unified model:

```text
App
 ├─ Installation
 └─ Instance
       │
       └─ Contributions
            ├─ Action
            ├─ Capability
            ├─ Context Provider
            ├─ Artifact Handler
            ├─ Deep Link Route
            ├─ Event
            └─ Suggested Task

Resource
 └─ ResourceRef
       │
       ├─ Context
       ├─ Invocation
       ├─ Artifact
       ├─ Event
       └─ Deep Link

Invocation
 ├─ Actor
 ├─ Capability
 ├─ Target Instance
 ├─ Context / Resource Bindings
 ├─ Command / Revision semantics
 └─ Result or TaskHandle
```

---

# 1. The highest principle of Stage 21

From now on:

# **What is shared across apps is the Semantic Contract, not the Domain Model.**

That is to say:

ArcChat can know:

```text
ArcNotes exposes:
Create Document
Read Document
Search Documents
```

But ArcChat:

# `Document` Domain Entity that does not own ArcNotes.

Likewise:

ArcChat can know:

```text
ArcSlate exposes:
Move Clip
Trim Clip
Start Render
```

But ArcChat:

# ArcSlate Timeline Domain is not referenced.

---

# 2. Cross-App Model is not a "universal dynamic RPC"

Continue the old idea of clearly deleting the general outline:

```text
invoke(
    string capability,
    Dictionary<string, object>
)
```

It cannot become an actual business agreement.

Nor can:

```text
resource.GetProperty("x")
resource.SetProperty("y", ...)
```

Flatten all products into dynamic objects.

The final pattern is still:

# **Shared semantic primitives + Owner-specific strongly typed contracts.**

---

# 3. Why is this particularly important?

Because ArcNotes, ArcScope, and ArcSlate are not the same type of software at all.

For example:

```text
ArcNotes.Document
```

and:

```text
ArcScope.Session
```

and:

```text
ArcSlate.Sequence
```

There is no reason to inherit:

```text
ArcForgesUniversalDocument
```

Such a huge common model.

All they need in common is:

```text
Identity
Reference
Capability
Invocation
Revision
Task
Provenance
Health
Compatibility
```

These platform semantics.

---

# 4. Formal definition of App

From a cross-application platform perspective:

# **App = a stable ArcForges product identity.**

Current official AppId:

```text
arcchat

arcnotes

arcscope

arcslate
```

---

# 5. AppId is always stable

For example:

```text
ArcNotes 1.0
ArcNotes 4.2
```

Still:

```text
AppId = arcnotes
```

Cannot:

```text
arcnotes-v2
```

As product versions change.

---

# 6. AppId ≠ ProductScope

Do not create repetitive concepts here.

## AppId

Solution:

> Which app owns/offers this thing?

For example:

```text
arcnotes
```

## ProductScope

Stage 0 commercial/entitlement use:

> Which product business scope does this subscription/feature fall into?

The two are related, but:

# Not the same Domain Concept.

---

# 7. AppId ≠ Process

Continuing with the general outline:

> `AppId` Stable, `InstanceId` unique for each startup.

So:

```text
ArcNotes
AppId = arcnotes
```

Launch today:

```text
Instance A
```

Shut down and then restart:

```text
Instance B
```

Still the same app.

---

# 8. AppInstallation must exist independently

Stage 13 has been frozen:

```text
App
≠
Installation
≠
Instance
```

Now officially included in the cross-app model.

---

## App

Product Identity.

```text
ArcNotes
```

---

## Installation

Installation on a device.

For example:

```text
ArcNotes installation
on DEKU Desktop
```

Its life cycle can span:

# Run multiple times.

---

## Instance

A running App Process.

For example:

```text
ArcNotes instance
started 14:22
```

Process ends:

# Instance ends.

---

# 9. Formal definition of Instance

# **AppInstance = the currently running instance that can actually provide local Capabilities.**

At least semantically:

```text
App identity

Instance identity

Installation identity

Device identity

App/build version

Contribution set

Health

Readiness

Compatibility
```

But:

> These are cross-App coordination metadata.

Does not include:

# Professional App Domain State.

---

# 10. Instance can have multiple Window/Document Sessions

Continuing with Stage 14 and general outline:

```text
One Process
    │
    ├─ Window A
    ├─ Window B
    └─ Window C
```

Still:

# An instance.

Therefore:

```text
WindowId
```

Not a substitute for:

```text
InstanceId
```

---

# 11. An App can have multiple Instances at the same time

For example in the future:

```text
ArcNotes Instance A

ArcNotes Instance B
```

Totally allowed.

So all routing systems start with:

# Cannot assume that AppId → unique Process.

The original general outline has also made it clear that random routing cannot be performed when multiple instances of the same product exist.

---

# 12. "Provider" is no longer used as the main product term of App Instance in cross-App

This is worth unifying now.

Because Stage 17 already exists:

# AI Provider

For example model supplier.

If App Instance is also called:

```text
Provider
```

A large number of logs/UI/API will be generated later:

> Is the Provider OpenAI or ArcNotes?

Therefore Stage 21 formally recommends:

# **App Instance / Capability Host**

as cross-App semantics.

`Provider` Reserved in preference to:

# AI Provider / external provider context.

Provider terminology already exists within the old master program and can be gradually migrated without changing the communication scheme.

---

# 13. App Contribution Model

An ArcForges App can contribute to the ecosystem:

```text
AppContribution
│
├── Capabilities
├── Actions
├── Context Providers
├── Artifact Handlers
├── Deep Link Routes
├── Events
└── Suggested Tasks
```

This becomes the basic way for ArcChat to understand an App.

---

# 14. ArcChat cannot hardcode all App behaviors

Error:

```text
switch (appId)
{
    case "arcnotes":
        ...
    case "arcscope":
        ...
    case "arcslate":
        ...
}
```

Found throughout:

```text
Agent
Home
Context menu
Artifact
Task
Search
```

---

Correct:

```text
App registers contributions
↓
Hub catalogs contributions
↓
ArcChat consumes contribution model
```

Added a fifth App:

> ArcChat core should not require extensive modifications.

---

# 15. Contribution is description, not authority

For example ArcNotes declares:

```text
Capability:
Create Document
```

Only represents:

> ArcNotes supports this semantic capability.

It does not mean:

# The caller automatically gets write permission.

Finally:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Risk
Approval
Resource ownership
```

Still handled by normal security systems.

Stage 26 completes the security policy.

---

# 16. Formal definition of Capability

# **Capability = A stable semantic capability provided externally by an App that can be called by the machine.**

It answers:

> What can this app do for the platform?

For example:

```text
arcnotes.document.create

arcnotes.document.read

arcscope.session.analyze

arcscope.measurement.run

arcslate.timeline.trim

arcslate.render.start
```

These are just naming style examples.

The specific ID set will be designed by the product contract later.

---

# 17. Capability must have a stable identity

Cannot be used:

```text
MoveClipAsync
```

This C# method name itself serves as the only long-term business identity.

Because:

```text
C# interface method

≠

Platform semantic identity
```

---

Strongly typed RPC methods certainly work:

```text
MoveClipAsync(...)
```

But it corresponds to a stable:

# CapabilityId.

This way:

* Agent;
* Permission;
* Audit;
* Compatibility;
* UI Action;
* Task Trace;

Both quoted:

# CapabilityId

rather than a CLR method string.

---

# 18. CapabilityId should be Namespaced

Conceptually:

```text
arcnotes.document.create

arcscope.session.compare

arcslate.timeline.split
```

Avoid:

```text
Create
Read
Move
Export
```

Such a global conflict.

---

# 19. Capability is business semantics, not CRUD mechanical mapping

Do not force all apps to be:

```text
CreateResource
UpdateResource
DeleteResource
ExecuteResourceOperation
```

This kind of interface completely loses the meaning of the domain.

---

Should:

ArcNotes:

```text
CreateDocument
InsertBlocks
UpdateProperties
```

ArcScope:

```text
CompareSessions
RunMeasurement
CreateFinding
```

ArcSlate:

```text
TrimClip
RippleDelete
StartRender
```

---

# 20. Capability cannot be equal to UI Command

For example:

```text
Zoom Timeline
Open Inspector
Toggle Sidebar
```

Most belong to:

# Local UI Command.

There is no need to expose it to the ecology.

---

Cross-App Capability should mean:

# Domain behaviors that have cross-application value.

---

# 21. Do not establish three different systems for Capability classification

We can distinguish semantically:

### Query

```text
Read-only
```

For example:

```text
ReadDocument
QuerySignals
GetTimeline
```

---

### Command

There are clear, relatively short-term business changes:

```text
AddTag
MoveClip
CreateMarker
```

---

### Long-running Capability

For example:

```text
RenderVideo
AnalyzeCapture
LargeExport
```

Return:

# TaskHandle / Child Task.

---

But these three:

# It's all Capability.

No need to create:

```text
QueryRegistry
CommandRegistry
TaskRegistry
```

Three sets of catalogs.

---

# 22. Capability Descriptor must express execution semantics

Rather than writing a specific DTO right now, each Capability must be able to describe:

```text
Capability identity

Owner App

Contract version

Input/output semantic contract

Accepted context/resource kinds

Execution shape

Effect semantics

Retry/idempotency semantics

Cancellation semantics

Preview support

Checkpoint/compensation support

Risk/security metadata

Feature requirements
```

---

# 23. Execution Shape

At least know:

```text
Immediate / bounded

Long-running / Task-producing
```

The caller cannot rely on:

> "How many seconds should this RPC take to complete?"

Guess.

---

# 24. Effect Semantics

In order to connect with Stage 19 and 26, Capability can at least state:

```text
Read-only

Reversible write

Compensatable write

Irreversible / external effect

Security-sensitive
```

The specific Risk Level continues to Stage 26.

---

# 25. Retry Semantics

At least you must know:

```text
Safe to retry

Idempotent with CommandId

Requires reconciliation

Must not blind retry
```

---

Because:

```text
ReadDocument
```

and:

```text
SendEmail
```

Never use the same Retry strategy.

Stage 19 has officially frozen the separation of `CommandId` and `AttemptId`; the general outline also makes it clear that writing commands can only be safely retried after the CommandId is idempotent.

---

# 26. Cancellation Semantics

Capability should be able to express:

```text
Cancelable

Cancelable at safe point

Not cancelable once committed
```

In this way, Stage 19 Task Runtime does not need to guess.

---

# 27. Preview / Preflight

Some capabilities can provide:

# Impact Preview.

For example:

```text
ArcNotes:
Replace 12 blocks

ArcSlate:
Ripple delete 34 clips
```

This pair:

```text
Approval
Agent preview
Diff
```

Very important.

---

However:

> Preview itself does not mean that Permission has been obtained.

---

# 28. Checkpoint Support

Capability can explain:

```text
Can create owner checkpoint
```

For example:

```text
ArcNotes large edit

ArcSlate major timeline edit
```

Task Runtime can therefore:

```text
Create checkpoint
↓
apply changes
```

---

# 29. Compensation Support

Capability can describe:

```text
Compensation available
```

For example:

```text
CreateDocument
→ move created document to Trash
```

But:

> Compensation is not a cross-process database transaction.

Continue to Stage 19.

---

# 30. Capability Metadata cannot reveal specific internal implementation

For example there is no need to tell ArcChat:

```text
Uses SQLite
Uses FFmpeg
Uses class TimelineService
```

These all belong to the Owner.

---

# 31. Formal definition of Action

# **Action = A context-sensitive executable entry displayed to the user.**

This is the most important difference between it and Capability.

---

For example, when the user selects ArcScope Session:

The Context Menu may display:

```text
Ask ArcChat

Create report in ArcNotes

Compare with...

Export...
```

These are:

# Actions.

---

# 32. Action ≠ Capability

An Action can:

### Directly corresponds to a Capability

```text
Add Marker
```

---

### Create a Task

```text
Analyze with ArcChat
```

---

### Trigger Handoff / Deep Link

```text
Open in ArcNotes
```

---

### Combine multiple capabilities

```text
Create Technical Report
```

---

Therefore:

# Action is the user experience layer semantics.

Capability:

# It is the execution layer semantics.

---

# 33. Not every Capability must be displayed as Action

For example internally:

```text
GetCurrentRevision
```

Agent/runtime may be required.

In the user menu:

> No need to show up.

---

# 34. Not every Action has only one Capability

For example:

```text
Create report in ArcNotes
```

Possible:

```text
Read ArcScope result
↓
Create ArcNotes document
↓
Open document
```

Completed by Task/Orchestration.

---

# 35. Action Descriptor should express

Conceptually at least:

```text
Action identity

Display semantics

Applicable context

Required capability/features

Execution style

Target App

Availability
```

The specific icon/text belongs to UI metadata.

---

# 36. Action availability is dynamic Projection

Same one:

```text
Open in ArcSlate
```

At this moment it may be:

```text
Available
```

Next moment:

```text
ArcSlate not installed
```

The next moment:

```text
Installed but incompatible
```

The Action itself has not changed.

What changes is:

# Availability.

---

# 37. Availability can at least express

```text
Available

Requires Launch

Requires Permission

Requires Selection / Context

Busy

Unavailable

Not Installed

Incompatible
```

---

Do not all fail:

```text
Disabled = true
```

Users do not know why.

---

# 38. PermissionRequired Action should not be hidden forever

For example:

```text
Delete Document
```

The user now has no permanent grant.

Still possible:

> See this Action.

Click:

# Enter the normal Approval/Permission process.

Otherwise users will feel:

> The functionality simply does not exist.

---

# 39. Context Provider formal definition

# **Context Provider = An App that exposes a read-only context source of "what the user is currently focusing on" to ArcChat/Agent.**

For example ArcNotes:

```text
Current Document

Current Selection

Current Block

Current Notebook
```

ArcScope:

```text
Current Session

Selected Time Range

Selected Signals

Current Comparison
```

ArcSlate:

```text
Current Sequence

Selected Clips

Playhead

In/Out Range
```

---

# 40. Context Provider ≠ Resource Database

Cannot:

```text
GetAllArcNotesData()
```

Then call:

# Context Provider.

Context should be:

# Current / Relevant / Bounded.

For complete query go to:

# Query Capability / Search.

---

# 41. Context Provider only provides "context description and reference"

Return first:

```text
ResourceRef

Selection / Slice

Metadata

Current revision
```

instead of:

> Copy the entire Document/Session/Video to ArcChat.

---

# 42. Context must distinguish between Stable and Ephemeral

This is very important design.

For example:

```text
ArcNotes DocumentRef
```

Relatively stable.

And:

```text
Current Selection
```

Extremely temporary.

The user may change Selection in the next second.

---

# 43. Ephemeral Context must be bound to Instance

For example:

```text
ArcSlate Current Selection
```

What it really means is:

> ArcSlate Instance A Selection at some point in time.

One cannot be saved permanently:

```text
CurrentSelection
```

Then continue using it after three hours.

---

# 44. Ephemeral Context should have Generation / Expiry semantics

No need to design specific fields now.

But you must be able to judge:

```text
still current

stale

instance gone
```

---

# 45. The temporary Context must be Freeze before the Task is created.

Stage 19 has stipulated that Task input cannot be saved forever:

```text
CurrentSelection
```

Such a dynamic concept.

Therefore:

```text
Current ArcScope Selection
```

When creating a Task, it resolves to:

```text
SessionRef

Selected SignalRefs

Time range

Revision / snapshot context
```

Then:

# This time the Task input is fixed.

---

# 46. Context Freeze ≠ Copy All Data

Still:

# Stable references + typed selection.

Not a copy:

```text
30GB capture
```

Enter Task.

---

# 47. A Context that cannot be Freeze cannot be pretended to be persistent.

For example:

> A completely instantaneous UI hover state that cannot be reproduced by the Owner.

This kind of Context:

# For immediate use only.

Automation that will be executed after three hours cannot be placed.

---

# 48. Context Provider does not grant read permissions

Even ArcChat knows:

```text
CurrentDocument = Document X
```

Does not mean:

> ArcChat automatically has permission to read the full text of X.

Actual reading:

# Still passes normal Capability + Authorization.

---

# 49. Context Provider cannot secretly expand Scope

User choice:

```text
Selected 3 blocks
```

Providers cannot:

> Easily return to the entire Notebook text.

---

# 50. Formal definition of Resource

# **Resource = A stably identifiable business object or asset owned by an authoritative Owner App.**

For example:

ArcNotes:

```text
Notebook
Document
Block
Attachment
```

ArcScope:

```text
Project
Session
Capture
Signal
Report
```

ArcSlate:

```text
Project
Sequence
MediaAsset
Clip
RenderOutput
```

---

# 51. Not all Domain Entities need to be cross-App Resources

For example, something inside ArcSlate:

```text
Bezier control handle
```

There is absolutely no need to become:

# Global Resource.

Only if:

```text
Cross-app reference value
stable identity value
User meaning
```

The object should be a Resource.

---

# 52. Formal definition of ResourceRef

# **ResourceRef = A stable, lightweight, non-directly writable reference to a Resource in the Owner App.**

It answers:

> "Whose, what, which one is that thing?"

It does not answer:

> "What is the complete content of that thing?"

---

# 53. The core semantics that ResourceRef must be able to express

I do not specify the specific fields now, but at least there are:

```text
Owner App

Resource kind/type

Stable Resource identity

Authority / Realm / Workspace scope when relevant

Optional revision semantics
```

and necessary:

# Resource availability hint.

---

# 54. ResourceKind should be Namespaced

For example conceptually:

```text
arcnotes.document

arcnotes.block

arcscope.session

arcscope.signal

arcslate.sequence

arcslate.media
```

---

Cannot be used globally:

```text
Document
Project
Item
```

Because:

```text
ArcNotes Project?
ArcScope Project?
ArcSlate Project?
```

will conflict.

---

# 55. ResourceRef does not allow the use of FilePath as an identity

Prohibited:

```text
ResourceRef =
C:\Projects\xxx...
```

Stage 14 has been frozen:

> Deep Link does not use absolute paths as stable identities.

Stage 20 also freezes:

```text
MediaAsset ≠ FilePath
```

The same applies.

---

# 56. ResourceRef is not allowed to contain

```text
ProcessId

Native pointer

GPU handle

SQLite row pointer

ViewModel

Window control

raw object reference
```

These all belong to:

# Inside the Owner runtime.

---

# 57. ResourceId will never be reused.

The general outline of the continuation has been determined:

> ResourceId is not reused, and file movement/renaming does not change the stable logical identity.

---

# 58. Resource Rename does not change ResourceRef

For example:

```text
ArcNotes:
Motor Report
↓
Motor Regression Report
```

Still:

# The same ResourceRef.

---

# 59. Resource Move does not change ResourceRef

For example:

```text
Notebook A
↓
Notebook B
```

If product semantics allow movement:

# Resource identity is maintained.

Specific changes in Ownership Scope are handled by the Owner.

---

# 60. After deleting the resource, ResourceRef should not automatically become a normal string.

For example, ArcNotes Document enters Trash:

Ref:

# Still exists.

Parsing status:

```text
Deleted / unavailable
```

---

After Restore:

# The original Ref is valid again.

This is consistent with the principle of maintaining DocumentId in Stage 15 Restore.

---

# 61. Copy/Import is the new Resource

For example:

```text
ArcScope Report
↓
Create editable document in ArcNotes
```

Finally:

```text
ArcNotes Document
```

Owns:

# new ResourceId.

and retain:

```text
Provenance → ArcScope ReportRef
```

Two Apps cannot share a writable Resource.

---

# 62. ResourceRef and RevisionRef must distinguish semantics

Normal:

```text
ResourceRef
```

Usually means:

# this resource.

---

Some tasks require:

```text
Resource at Revision 42
```

This is equivalent to:

# Pinned Resource Version.

---

# 63. Floating Ref and Pinned Ref cannot be mixed

For example:

> "Open this Document"

Typically used:

# Current ResourceRef.

And:

> "Why did Agent make this judgment this time?"

Provenance may require:

# Revision-bound Ref.

---

```text
Structured analysis
```

a:

itself is:

# 91. Formal definition of Event

# **Event = an observable fact that has occurred.**

For example:

```text
DocumentCreated

CaptureCompleted

RenderCompleted

TaskCompleted

ResourceDeleted
```

---

# 92. Event ≠ Command

Cannot:

```text
Event:
PleaseDeleteDocument
```

This is actually:

# Command.

---

Real Event:

```text
DocumentDeleted
```

means:

# has happened.

---

# 93. Event must be generated after business facts are submitted

For example ArcNotes:

```text
Domain state committed
↓
Revision 43
↓
DocumentUpdated Event
```

Cannot:

```text
Event emitted
↓
database write later failed
```

Otherwise the downstream will see:

> Something that did not happen at all.

---

# 94. Event should have stable EventId

Reason:

# At-least-once delivery.

The same Event may:

> Received twice due to reconnection/retries.

Consumer:

# Remove duplicates by EventId.

---

# 95. Event requires Causation / Correlation

For example:

```text
Automation
↓
Task
↓
ArcNotes CreateDocument
↓
DocumentCreated Event
```

Event should know:

```text
caused by Task / Command
```

This way Stage 19 can:

# Anti-Automation Loop.

---

# 96. Event should quote Resource instead of copying huge text

Correct:

```text
CaptureCompleted

SessionRef
CaptureRef
Revision
summary metadata
```

---

Incorrect:

```text
Event payload
=
18GB capture bytes
```
